readerTitle: Why Zappos started without a single shoe in stock
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Zappos 초기) + 가상 적용 (가정 유지보수 서비스, 베이커리·컨설턴트·소매점 예시)
insight: MVP는 기능을 줄인 작은 제품이 아니라, 가장 중요한 질문에 실제 고객의 행동으로 답하는 가장 싼 실험이다.
misconception: MVP는 기능을 덜어 낸 첫 버전이거나, 싸고 대충 만든 제품이다.

sources.text: Ries, E. (2011). The Lean Startup. Crown Business. (Zappos 초기 사례, MVP 정의)
Amazon press release on the Zappos acquisition (2009)
Frank Robinson (SyncDev), 'minimum viable product' 용어 최초 사용 (2001년경)

factChecks.note: Nick Swinmurn이 1999년에 지역 신발 매장에서 신발 사진을 찍어 웹사이트에 올리고, 주문이 들어오면 매장에서 정가로 사서 배송했다는 내용은 Ries(2011)에 나옵니다. 원문 표현을 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.
'He made little or nothing on each pair'는 정가로 사서 판매했다는 서술에서 나온 추정입니다. 실제 판매가와 마진은 확인되지 않았으므로 단정 표현을 피했습니다.
Amazon의 Zappos 인수는 2009년 발표(같은 해 완료)입니다. 인수 금액은 기준에 따라 다르게 보도되어 카드에 적지 않았습니다.
MVP 용어는 Frank Robinson이 처음 썼고 Eric Ries가 대중화했습니다. 카드에는 Ries의 정의를 직접 인용하지 않고 풀어 썼습니다.

cards.title: Why Zappos started without a single shoe in stock
body: In 1999, a young man walked into shoe stores with a camera. He wasn't a customer. He wasn't a journalist.
He was testing a business that didn't exist yet, and he didn't own a single pair of shoes to sell.

image.label: A person photographing shoes on a store shelf
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 1990년대 분위기의 신발 매장 진열대 앞에서 한 사람이 필름 카메라로 운동화 한 켤레를 찍고 있음. 뒤편에 작은 노트북 화면에 같은 신발 사진이 떠 있는 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You think people will buy shoes online.
body: It's the late 1990s. Friends say nobody will buy shoes they can't try on. You have modest savings and a strong hunch.
What do you do first?

options.text: Lease a small warehouse, stock popular styles and build a proper website
options.feedback: You'd be ready to sell, but you'd spend most of your savings before learning whether anyone buys. If the hunch is wrong, the money is gone.

options.text: Survey 500 people about whether they'd buy shoes online
options.feedback: Cheap and fast. But saying yes costs people nothing. You'd learn their opinions, not what they do with their own money.

options.text: Post photos of shoes from local stores and buy each pair only after someone orders it
options.feedback: You give up profit and efficiency for now. In return, real customers answer your biggest question with real orders, at almost no risk.

cards.title: The store shelves were the warehouse.
body: Nick Swinmurn photographed shoes at local stores and put the pictures on a simple website. When an order came in, he went back to the store, bought the pair at full price and mailed it.
He likely made little or nothing on each pair. That wasn't the point. Every order proved that strangers would pay for shoes they had never touched.
The company became Zappos. In 2009, Amazon bought it.

cards.title: The minimum viable product
body: A **minimum viable product (MVP)** is the smallest version of an idea that real customers can actually use or buy, built to answer your most important question.
Eric Ries made the term popular in *The Lean Startup* (2011). His point: the first goal isn't to sell a lot. It's to learn the most with the least effort.
Swinmurn's MVP was a few photos and a promise to deliver.

image.label: A big question mark next to a small, simple product
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 큰 물음표 "Will people buy shoes they can't try on?", 오른쪽에 아주 작은 상자 하나(사진 몇 장이 붙은 간단한 웹페이지). 둘 사이를 화살표로 연결하고 "Smallest thing that answers it" 라벨. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Minimum for you, viable for them.
body: Three choices shape a good MVP.
list: **The question:** what must be true for this to work? For Zappos: people will buy shoes they can't try on.
**Minimum:** cut everything that doesn't help answer it. No warehouse, no stock, no custom software.
**Viable:** keep what the customer touches. Real shoes, real prices, real delivery.
cards.callout: Minimum is about your effort. Viable is about the customer's experience.
cards.softwareNote: A software MVP is often one core feature for one type of user, with payment switched on from day one. The signal is whether people come back and pay, not how many sign up.

cards.title: An MVP can take many shapes.
body: A baker sells a new pastry for one Saturday before buying an oven for it. A consultant sells one fixed-price workshop before writing a full program. A shop stocks ten units of a new product line before ordering a thousand.
Each one shares two things: real customers make a real choice, and the business can stop cheaply if the answer is no.

image.label: Three small tests: a pastry tray, a workshop flyer, a short shelf
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 세 칸 구성: 빵 한 쟁반과 "Saturday only" 팻말, 워크숍 전단 한 장, 상품 열 개만 놓인 작은 선반. 각 칸 아래 작은 "Yes / No" 표시. 실제 브랜드 없음.

cards.title: Minimum is not the same as sloppy.
body: If the test is too rough, a "no" may mean you ran a bad test, not that you had a bad idea. Late shoes or blurry photos would have told Swinmurn nothing about online shoe buying.
Some things can't be minimal: food safety, licensed work, anything that could hurt someone.
And an MVP answers early questions only. Zappos still had to learn warehouses, returns and margins later.

cards.title: Now it's a home repair business.
body: You're an electrician with loyal customers. You want to offer a monthly home maintenance plan: two visits a year, priority call-outs, small fixes included.
Your biggest question is whether homeowners will pay every month for this. What's your MVP?

options.text: Buy a second van, hire two technicians and build a booking app
options.feedback: You'd be ready for growth, but you'd carry big costs before knowing if anyone pays monthly. That's a launch, not a test.

options.text: Offer a one-page plan to 30 past customers, do the visits yourself, and charge from month one
options.feedback: It won't scale and it takes your own time. But paying customers answer the exact question, and you can stop or adjust cheaply.

options.text: Give the plan free for three months to past customers and ask for feedback
options.feedback: You'll learn what they like about the service. But free hides the one thing you need to know: whether they'll pay for it.

cards.title: Build the smallest thing that answers your biggest question.
body: An MVP isn't a cheap first version of your product. It's a real offer, cut down to the one thing you need to learn.
**Try it today:** write your idea's biggest question in one sentence. Then list what you could remove and still get a real customer to say yes or no.
